selection.rule: Dependency-complete first 24 questions from the question-sheet selection order.

questions.question: What issue does the passage introduce about the daily prayers?
questions.answer: It introduces the complaint that praying five times every day feels too much and becomes tiring because it keeps repeating.

questions.question: How is the man who raised this complaint described?
questions.answer: He is described as someone advanced in age, strong in body, and high in social position.

questions.question: When the speaker later examined himself, what did he hear from his nafs?
questions.answer: He found that his nafs was saying the very same complaint about the prayers.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest was influencing the nafs?
questions.answer: It suggests that laziness opened it to Satan’s influence and teaching.

questions.question: What broader conclusion does the speaker draw from hearing the same words in his nafs?
questions.answer: He concludes that the complaint represents the voice of souls that push people toward wrong, not just one individual’s opinion.

questions.question: Why does the speaker decide to begin with himself rather than with others?
questions.answer: He realizes that a person who has not corrected his own nafs is not ready to guide other people.

questions.question: What kind of response does the speaker choose to give to his nafs?
questions.answer: He chooses to give it five warnings.

questions.question: What do the phrases about idleness, heedlessness, and compounded ignorance show about the speaker’s judgment of the complaint?
questions.answer: They show that he sees the complaint as spiritually unhealthy, careless, and based on confused thinking rather than sound understanding.

questions.question: What Qur’anic teaching is mentioned near the beginning of the passage?
questions.answer: It says that prayer has been required for believers at specific appointed times.

questions.question: What specific objection does the man make about praying?
questions.answer: He says prayer itself is good, but doing it five times every day without end feels excessive and exhausting.

questions.question: Why is it important that the speaker later hears the same objection within himself?
questions.answer: It shows honesty and self-awareness, because he recognizes that the struggle is not only in other people but also inside his own soul.

questions.question: What does “with the ear of laziness” suggest about how the nafs was listening?
questions.answer: It suggests the nafs was listening in a careless, comfort-loving way that made it more open to bad whispers.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is one sign that these thoughts are spiritually dangerous?
questions.answer: They are linked to the evil-commanding self and to satanic prompting.

questions.question: What principle of self-reform is stated in the passage?
questions.answer: A person must work on fixing his own nafs before trying to reform others.

questions.question: What mood or tone does the speaker use when addressing his nafs at the end of the passage?
questions.answer: He speaks in a serious, corrective, and warning tone, preparing to confront it directly.

questions.question: What does the final sentence prepare the reader for?
questions.answer: It prepares the reader for a structured reply made up of five separate warnings.

questions.question: Who first voices the complaint about the prayers in this passage?
questions.answer: An older, physically impressive, and socially important man voices it first.

questions.question: What exactly makes the man say the prayers become hard to keep up with?
questions.answer: He thinks their daily repetition never ends, so he feels worn out by them.

questions.question: How much time passes before the speaker revisits those words within himself?
questions.answer: A long time passes before he reflects and hears the same thing from his nafs.

questions.question: Why does the speaker treat the complaint as more than just one man’s personal opinion?
questions.answer: Because he recognizes the same attitude in his own nafs, so he sees it as a wider human struggle.

questions.question: What does the statement about not reforming others unless one reforms oneself teach about leadership?
questions.answer: It teaches that real guidance starts with self-discipline and sincerity, not just speaking to others.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the five warnings the speaker plans to give?
questions.answer: Their purpose is to answer, challenge, and correct the nafs for its lazy and heedless objection.

questions.question: What can we infer about the speaker’s method of dealing with spiritual weakness?
questions.answer: He deals with it through reflection, honesty, and direct moral instruction aimed first at himself.

questions.question: In summary, what is the main lesson of this passage section?
questions.answer: The main lesson is that complaints against regular prayer often come from the undisciplined nafs, so a believer should begin by reforming himself with honest self-warning.
